title: McGuffey's Fifth Eclectic Reader
sourceTitle: McGuffey's Fifth Eclectic Reader, Revised Edition
author: William Holmes McGuffey
licenseEvidence: Project Gutenberg eBook #15040: 'Public domain in the USA.' Revised edition first copyrighted 1879 (Van Antwerp, Bragg & Co.); renewals 1896 (American Book Company) and 1907 and 1920 (H. H. Vail), all before 1930.
description: The classic Fifth Reader: 117 selections from Irving, Longfellow, Whittier, Dickens, Shakespeare, Audubon, and many more, from 'The Village Blacksmith' to 'William Tell' and the passenger pigeon. Each day your child learns a few words from the lesson, reads it aloud with expression, and writes a short narration or memorizes a poem; a short course in elocution opens the year. The full text is free online.
includes: 123 lessons in 13 units: 6 elocution lessons plus all 117 Fifth Reader selections
Link to the free full text for every lesson
Vocabulary from each lesson's own definitions, plus a read-aloud and narration activity each day
Short written narration prompts for prose and memory work for poems
Author notes and parent notes on dated content

lessons.title: Elocution: Preliminary Remarks and Articulation
steps: Read the Preliminary Remarks together and put Rule 1 in your own words
Say the vocals, subvocals, and aspirates in the tables aloud; feel the difference between cognate pairs like b/p and v/f
Read the 'Faults to Be Remedied' examples, saying the incorrect form and then the correct one
Practice five of the Exercises in Articulation sentences until each is crisp and clear
questions: What is the great object of reading aloud, according to the book?
What is the difference between a subvocal and an aspirate?
Name one common fault in articulation the book warns about.
answers: To give the hearer the writer's ideas and feelings fully and clearly
A subvocal uses the voice with the breath partly blocked; an aspirate is breath only
Dropping unaccented vowels (sep'rate for separate), dropping final sounds (an' for and), or running words together
lessons.notes: The Fifth Reader opens with a short course in elocution. Treat these lessons as voice practice, not memorization; come back to them as warm-ups all year.

lessons.title: Elocution: Inflections
steps: Read the definitions of rising and falling inflection and practice 'Did you walk or ride?' several ways
Work through the rules for the falling inflection (complete sense, strong emphasis, commencing and concluding series)
Practice the rising inflection on yes-or-no questions and on direct address
Try the circumflex and monotone examples and talk about when each would be used
questions: Which inflection usually goes on a question that can be answered yes or no?
Which inflection is usual when the sense of a sentence is complete?
What is a monotone, and when does the book say to use it?
answers: The rising inflection
The falling inflection
Reading on one unchanging note; for solemn or awe-filled passages
lessons.notes: Long section; it is fine to split it over two days. The book marks inflections with accent marks that may look like plain apostrophes in the online text.

lessons.title: Elocution: Accent and Emphasis
steps: Read about accent and say the word pairs whose meaning changes with the accent (like CON-duct and con-DUCT)
Read about emphasis; say one sentence several times, stressing a different word each time, and talk about how the meaning shifts
Practice the absolute and relative emphasis examples and the emphatic pause
questions: What is the difference between accent and emphasis?
What is 'relative emphasis'?
answers: Accent is stress on a syllable within a word; emphasis is stress on a word or phrase within a sentence
Emphasis that brings out a contrast between two words or ideas

lessons.title: Elocution: Modulation and Poetic Pauses
steps: Read about pitch and compass; find your own comfortable keynote and read a paragraph on it
Practice the voice exercise from Remark 5: the same lines at low, middle, and high pitch, without getting louder
Read about quantity and quality, then try the examples in a soft, a full, and a harsh tone
Read about the final and caesural pauses and read the Marmion lines both ways
questions: What is the 'compass' of the voice?
What two faults of pitch does the book warn about?
What is a caesural pause?
answers: The range of the voice above and below its keynote
Monotony (staying on one note) and changing pitch or force without regard to the sense, like singsong
A pause in the middle of a line of poetry

lessons.title: Elocution: Exercises I–III
steps: Read 'Death of Franklin' in a solemn tone, watching the marked inflections
Read 'Bonaparte' aloud, giving the falling inflection to each sharp contrast
Read Hamlet's lines on Yorick slowly and thoughtfully
Choose one of the three to read to the family with full expression
questions: Why does the Franklin passage say nations should mourn him?
Which writer's character is 'Hamlet on Seeing the Skull of Yorick' taken from?
answers: He was a benefactor of humanity, not merely a great man in rank
Shakespeare's Hamlet
lessons.notes: Short practice pieces with inflection marks. The Bonaparte passage is a harsh political portrait of Napoleon.

lessons.title: Elocution: Exercises IV–V
steps: Read the battle lines from Scott's Marmion with energy, letting the pace quicken
Read 'Lord Ullin's Daughter' aloud, marking your own inflections as the book suggests
Narrate the story of the chieftain, the lady, and the boatman
questions: Why are the chieftain and Lord Ullin's daughter fleeing?
What happens to them on the lake?
How does Lord Ullin feel at the end?
answers: Her father, Lord Ullin, and his men are chasing them
The boat is swamped by the storm and they drown
Full of grief and regret; he would forgive them if they came back
lessons.notes: Poems by Sir Walter Scott and Thomas Campbell. A sad ending: the lovers drown.

lessons.title: Lesson I: The Good Reader
steps: New words: petition (a formal request), articulate (to utter sounds clearly), monotony (lack of variety), concise (brief and full of meaning), dictate (to speak so another can write it down)
Read the story aloud, showing the difference between the two pages' bad reading and Ernestine's good reading
Written narration: in a paragraph, tell what went wrong with each page's reading and why Ernestine succeeded
questions: What was wrong with the first page's reading?
What was the widow's petition about?
What reward did the King give Ernestine?
answers: He ran his words together in a fast, dull monotone
Her delicate son had been drafted into the army, though he wanted to be a portrait painter
She carried the order for the son's discharge; later the King paid for her education and made her father chief gardener
lessons.notes: Frederick the Great ruled Prussia from 1740 to 1786. This story sets the theme of the whole book: read to make your listener understand and feel.

lessons.title: Lesson II: The Bluebell
steps: New words: rift (a narrow opening), chalice (a cup), bonny (beautiful)
Read the poem aloud gently, letting each three-line stanza flow
Memorize: the last stanza, 'The patient child whose watchful eye...'
Talk about the lesson the poet draws from the flower
questions: What color was the flower at first?
What did the flower watch every day and night?
What lesson does the poem give children?
answers: White as snow
The narrow strip of sky and one bright star
A child who keeps looking toward pure and high things will grow like them

lessons.title: Lesson III: The Gentle Hand
steps: New words: vicinity (neighborhood), potent (powerful), peremptory (commanding), ally (one who joins with another), crotchet (a whim)
Read the story aloud, using a rough voice for the farmer and a soft one for the girl
Written narration: in a paragraph, describe three times the girl's gentle hand changed things
questions: How did the girl quiet the big dog Tiger?
Why wouldn't the pony Dick move, and what finally made him go?
What did the farmer say was the secret of his daughter's power?
answers: She laid her hand on his neck and spoke a low word
He was stubborn; whipping and jerking failed, but the girl stroked him and spoke kindly
She's good; everybody and everything loves her
lessons.notes: By T. S. Arthur, a popular 19th-century writer of moral tales.

lessons.title: Lesson IV: The Grandfather
steps: New words: hale (healthy), manteltree (shelf over a fireplace), plodded (went slowly)
Read the poem aloud quietly, as a peaceful summer afternoon
Copywork: "Fast asleep were they both on that summer day."
Narrate: why did the grandfather really cry?
questions: What did the little girl think made her grandfather cry?
What was the real reason for his tear?
What was the grandmother doing?
answers: His pipe smoke
He remembered her dead mother sitting in the same place
Clearing away dinner and then spinning at the wheel
lessons.notes: Poem by Charles G. Eastman. Gently mentions a mother's death.

lessons.title: Lesson V: A Boy on a Farm
steps: New words: factotum (one who does all kinds of work), indispensable (absolutely necessary), economize (to save), dispatch (haste), chores (light household work)
Read the selection aloud, enjoying its humor
Written narration: in a paragraph, list the farm boy's jobs and tell which you would like least
List your own chores and see how they compare
questions: Why does the boy turn cartwheels along the road, according to the author?
Why does the boy take so long getting water from the spring?
What does the author think chores do for a boy?
answers: He's 'inventing a new way to travel' to save his legs
He stops to poke frogs and play with the water
They give him a real education and make him useful as a man
lessons.notes: By Charles Dudley Warner, from 'Being a Boy.' Humor and gentle exaggeration; a few period jobs (penstock, grindstone, stoning raisins) may need explaining.

lessons.title: Lesson VI: The Singing Lesson
steps: New words: sauntering (strolling), snicker (a half-hidden laugh), crest (a tuft on a bird's head), moral (the lesson a story teaches)
Read the poem aloud with expression, giving the dove a coaxing voice
Memorize: the first stanza, 'A nightingale made a mistake...'
Discuss the moral the poem asks you to find
questions: Why did the nightingale hide?
Who cheered her up?
When she sang again, where did she fix her eyes?
answers: She sang a few notes out of tune and was ashamed
A dove
On the sky, not on the people below
lessons.notes: Poem by Jean Ingelow. Nightingales live in Europe, not America.

lessons.title: Lesson VII: Do Not Meddle
steps: New words: aversion (dislike), consternation (dismay), principle (a right rule of conduct), integrity (honesty), legacy (a gift left by will)
Read the story aloud, pausing after each boy to guess what trap comes next
Written narration: in a paragraph, tell what happened to each of the seven boys
Discuss the old gentleman's saying about peeping into drawers
questions: What trap caught Henry Wilkins?
What happened when Rufus Wilson touched the drawer knob?
Why did Harry Gordon get the job?
answers: Fake cherries filled with cayenne pepper
A hidden bell rang loudly
He sat still for twenty minutes and touched nothing
lessons.notes: A pound was about $4.86 at the time. The 'electrical machine' trap is a 19th-century gadget; don't try it at home.

lessons.title: Lesson VIII: Work
steps: New words: mesh (network), rife (abounding), stagnant (inactive), torpor (laziness), lolls (lounges)
Read the poem aloud briskly and boldly, like a call to action
Memorize: the first stanza, 'Work, work, my boy, be not afraid...'
questions: What does the poet say there is in the shuttle's song and the anvil's stroke?
Who does the poet doubt enjoys his bread as much as a worker?
When is a man most blessed, according to the last stanza?
answers: Glory and triumph
The idle man who has plenty without working
When a busy day ends in a well-earned, contented rest
lessons.notes: Poem by Eliza Cook.

lessons.title: Lesson IX: The Maniac
steps: New words: exterior (outward look), revenues (income from taxes), deficit (shortfall), defaulter (one who can't account for money in his care), injunction (a command)
Read the story aloud in a low, serious voice
Narrate: how did a small arithmetic mistake ruin Conrad Lange?
questions: What phrase did the old man keep repeating?
What caused the shortage in his accounts?
What lesson does the last paragraph draw?
answers: "Once one is two"
A multiplication mistake: he figured once one is two
Our minds are easily overthrown if we rely only on this world; we should cast our cares on God
lessons.notes: A sad story about mental illness, told in old-fashioned terms ('maniac'). A ducat was a gold coin worth about $2.00.

lessons.title: Lesson X: Robin Redbreast
steps: Read the poem aloud, letting the refrain 'Robin, Robin Redbreast' sing
Compare the English robin (described in the note) with the American robin you know
Copywork: "Robin sings so sweetly / In the falling of the year."
questions: What season is the poem about?
What does the poet say the trees are like, and what will they turn into?
What does the last stanza ask us to give Robin?
answers: Late autumn, as summer ends
Indian princes in bright colors who will soon turn to ghosts
A crumb of bread to cheer him
lessons.notes: Poem by William Allingham. The European robin is a different, smaller bird than the American robin.

lessons.title: Lesson XI: The Fish I Didn't Catch
steps: New words: genial (cheerful), haunts (favorite places), propriety (proper behavior), anticipate (to take before the right time), achievement (a deed done)
Read the story aloud, with the uncle's calm voice and the boy's excitement
Written narration: in a paragraph, tell the story and explain the uncle's proverb in your own words
questions: How did the boy lose his first fish?
What advice did his uncle give him?
How does the author say a child's sorrow differs from a grown-up's?
answers: He shouted to his uncle before landing it, and it slipped off the hook into the stream
Never brag of your fish before you catch him
A child's grief is complete and unreasoning; adults hold theirs back with reason
lessons.notes: By John Greenleaf Whittier, the Quaker poet, remembering his boyhood.

lessons.title: Lesson XII: It Snows
steps: New words: trow (believe), imbecile (here, a feeble person), intervened (lay between), stifled (choked back)
Read the poem aloud, giving each speaker (schoolboy, invalid, traveler, belle, widow) a different voice
Narrate: how does each person feel about the snow, and why?
questions: Who shouts 'Hurrah!' at the snow?
Why is the traveler glad?
Why is the snow bitter for the widow?
answers: The schoolboy
He thinks of his warm home and family waiting
She is poor, with no food for her children and her last wood burning
lessons.notes: Poem by Sarah Josepha Hale, who also wrote 'Mary Had a Little Lamb.' 'Imbecile' here means someone weak and sickly, not an insult.

lessons.title: Lesson XIII: Respect for the Sabbath Rewarded
steps: New words: genteel (fashionable), violate (to break), dialect (local speech), identity (being who one claims), extremity (greatest need)
Read the story aloud, building suspense in the stranger's questions
Written narration: in a paragraph, tell how William Reed's choice led to his fortune
questions: Why did the barber lose his fashionable customers?
Why did he ask the stranger for a half-penny?
Who was the stranger, and what news did he bring?
answers: He stopped working on Sundays
To buy a candle, since it was too dark to shave safely
A lawyer searching for him; his uncle had died and left him a fortune
lessons.notes: Set in Bath, England. A moral tale about keeping Sunday; 'half a crown' was a British coin.

lessons.title: Lesson XIV: The Sands o' Dee
steps: New words: dank (damp), tress (a lock of hair)
Read the poem in a low, musical voice, varying the three repeated lines in each stanza as the book suggests
Memorize: the first stanza
questions: What was Mary sent to do?
What happened to her?
What do the boatmen still hear?
answers: Call the cattle home across the sands
The tide and mist came in and she drowned
Her voice calling the cattle home
lessons.notes: Poem by Charles Kingsley. The book calls the Dee a Scottish river; the famous Dee sands Kingsley wrote about are actually on the border of England and Wales. A sad poem about a drowning.

lessons.title: Lesson XV: Select Paragraphs
steps: New words: ordained (established), dominion (rule), haven (harbor)
Read the six Bible passages aloud slowly and reverently
Memorize: Psalm 23 (paragraph 6), if your child doesn't know it already
Find which psalm each paragraph comes from
questions: In paragraph 2, where does the psalmist say God has set man?
In paragraph 5, what do sailors do when they are at their wit's end?
In Psalm 23, what is the Lord compared to?
answers: A little lower than the angels, crowned with glory and honor
Cry to the Lord, who calms the storm
A shepherd
lessons.notes: Passages from the Psalms (King James Version): 105, 8, 91, 95/96, 107, and 23.

lessons.title: Lesson XVI: The Corn Song
steps: New words: hoard (a store laid up), lavish (generous), meads (meadows), vapid (dull), samp (boiled crushed corn)
Read the poem aloud with a hearty, harvest-festival spirit
Trace the corn through the seasons: April, May, June, autumn
Memorize: the first stanza
questions: Which crops does the poem say other lands may boast of?
What drove the crows from the sprouting grain?
What does the farmer thank God for at the end?
answers: Apples, oranges, and grapes
The farmers frightened them away
The golden corn
lessons.notes: Poem by John Greenleaf Whittier, from his 'Songs of Labor.'

lessons.title: Lesson XVII: The Venomous Worm
steps: New words: reptiles (crawling animals), infested (troubled), delirium (a wandering mind), paroxysm (a fit), still (a vessel for making liquor)
Read the lesson aloud, keeping the riddle a secret until the last line
Narrate: what is the 'worm' really, and why did the author describe it as a snake?
questions: What is the 'worm of the still'?
Which animals avoid this worm?
What does the bitten person do as soon as he recovers?
answers: The coiled pipe used to distill liquor; it stands for strong drink
All animals; only people are 'bitten'
Goes back to be bitten again
lessons.notes: By John Russell. A temperance piece written as a riddle. A good chance to talk about addiction in your own family's terms.

lessons.title: Lesson XVIII: The Festal Board
steps: New words: festal (joyous), enhance (increase), sundered (separated), felon (a criminal), lure (to tempt)
Read the poem aloud: lightly for the party, then slowly and sadly for what came after
Narrate: what happened to the guests after the feast?
questions: What became of the beautiful young woman?
Where is the strong young man now?
What does the poet blame for all these sorrows?
answers: She died of a broken heart
In prison, on a felon's bed
Too many feasts and drinking
lessons.notes: Another temperance poem; heavy themes of ruin and death. Golconda was an Indian city famous for diamonds.

lessons.title: Lesson XIX: How to Tell Bad News
steps: Read the dialogue aloud with two readers, one as Mr. H. and one as the Steward
Keep the Steward's voice matter-of-fact to bring out the joke
Retell the chain of bad news backward, from the bank failure to the magpie
questions: What was the first piece of 'bad news' the steward gave?
How did the father's house burn down?
Why is the steward's way of telling the news funny?
answers: The magpie was dead
From the torches at his mother's funeral
He starts with the smallest thing and works backward to the biggest disasters
lessons.notes: A comic dialogue. There are no definitions for this lesson.

lessons.title: Lesson XX: The Battle of Blenheim
steps: Read the poem aloud; give Kaspar a tired voice and the children curious ones
Find Bavaria on a map
Written narration: in a paragraph, tell what Kaspar knows about the battle and what he doesn't know
Discuss the poet's point in the repeated 'famous victory'
questions: What did Peterkin find by the stream?
Who won the battle?
What can't Kaspar explain?
answers: A skull from the battle
The English (with Prince Eugene) beat the French
What the war was for and what good came of it
lessons.notes: Poem by Robert Southey about the 1704 battle in the War of the Spanish Succession. Its point is anti-war irony; it mentions dead bodies and suffering civilians.

lessons.title: Lesson XXI: "I Pity Them"
steps: New words: emigrate (to move to a new place to live), predicament (plight), predominate (to prevail), destitute (needy), destination (journey's end)
Read the story aloud
Narrate: how did the westerner show that pity must be more than words?
questions: What happened to the family's horse?
What did the man from the West hold up?
What became of the emigrant family?
answers: It fell through a rotten bridge and drowned
A ten-dollar bill, 'the amount of my pity'
They reached Illinois and he became a thriving farmer

lessons.title: Lesson XXII: An Elegy on Madam Blaize
steps: New words: accord (agreement), pledge (property left as security for a loan), hangers-on (followers), mortal (deadly)
Read the poem aloud, pausing at each dash before the twist
Explain the joke in two of the stanzas
questions: Who did Madam Blaize lend money to?
When did she never sleep in church?
Why is the last stanza funny?
answers: To the poor, but only if they left a pledge
Except when she shut her eyes
It states the obvious: had she lived longer, she wouldn't have died today
lessons.notes: Poem by Oliver Goldsmith. A mock elegy: each stanza begins with praise and ends by undercutting it.

lessons.title: Lesson XXIII: King Charles II and William Penn
steps: New words: regiment (a body of soldiers), aggressors (those who strike first), venison (deer meat), excesses (misdeeds)
Read the dialogue with two readers, Penn speaking plainly in 'thee' and 'thou'
Written narration: in a paragraph, explain Penn's argument against the 'right of discovery'
questions: What did Penn depend on instead of soldiers?
How did Penn plan to get land from the Indians?
What imaginary situation did Penn use to change the King's mind?
answers: The Indians' own sense of justice
By buying it from them
Indians discovering Britain and claiming it for themselves
lessons.notes: By Mason L. Weems (Parson Weems). The King's words call Native Americans 'savages' and 'cannibals'; Penn argues against him. Talk about that dated language and the real history of Penn's treaties.

lessons.title: Lesson XXIV: What I Live For
steps: New words: emulate (to try to equal), wake (the track left behind a ship), bard (poet), martyr (one who suffers for a principle), sage (wise man)
Read the poem aloud with warmth and conviction
Memorize: the first stanza
Talk about which line best matches what you live for
questions: Whose story does the poet live to learn?
What kind of season does the poet hope for in stanza 3?
Which line ends both the first and last stanzas?
answers: Those who suffered for us: poets, patriots, martyrs, and sages
A time when people live by reason, not gold, and every wrong is righted
And the good that I can do
lessons.notes: Poem by George Linnaeus Banks (not named in the book).

lessons.title: Lesson XXV: The Righteous Never Forsaken
steps: New words: fagots (bundles of sticks), dissipate (to scatter), sustenance (food), fortitude (brave endurance), proffered (offered)
Read the story aloud, softly at first, then with joy at the surprise
Written narration: in a paragraph, tell the story from the traveler's point of view
questions: What was the only food the widow had left?
Why did she share it with the stranger?
Who was the stranger?
answers: One smoked herring
She hoped others would treat her own lost son the same way
Her long-lost eldest son, home rich from the Indies
lessons.notes: Quotes William Cowper's hymn 'God Moves in a Mysterious Way.'

lessons.title: Lesson XXVI: Abou Ben Adhem
steps: Read the poem aloud with quiet dignity
Memorize: the whole poem (it's only 18 lines)
Narrate: why did Ben Adhem's name lead all the rest?
questions: What was the angel writing?
What did Abou ask the angel to write for him?
What did the angel show him the next night?
answers: The names of those who love the Lord
Write me as one that loves his fellow men
The list of names blessed by God's love, with his name first
lessons.notes: Poem by Leigh Hunt, a classic for memorizing.

lessons.title: Lesson XXVII: Lucy Forester
steps: New words: brae (a hillside), brake (a thicket), reverberating (echoing), plaid (a Scottish shawl), scour (to search swiftly)
Read the story aloud in two sittings if needed, building suspense
Written narration: in a paragraph, tell how Lucy was lost and found
questions: Where was Lucy supposed to spend the day?
Why did Aunt Isabel believe Lucy was still alive?
Who found Lucy?
answers: At Ladyside, with the Mayne children
There were no signs of violence; the blood seemed put there to deceive, and a murderer would have taken the clothes
Jacob Mayne
lessons.notes: By John Wilson ('Christopher North'), set in Scotland. The kidnapping is blamed on a 'gypsy' woman; this is an old stereotype about the Romani people and is worth a short talk.

lessons.title: Lesson XXVIII: The Reaper and the Flowers
steps: New words: sheaves (bundles of grain), token (keepsake), transplanted (moved and replanted)
Read the poem aloud slowly and tenderly
Memorize: the first stanza
Discuss what the Reaper and the flowers stand for
questions: Who is the Reaper?
What do the flowers stand for?
How does the mother find comfort?
answers: Death
Little children who die
She knows she will find them again in heaven
lessons.notes: Poem by Henry Wadsworth Longfellow, about the death of children. Read it with care if your family has had a loss.

lessons.title: Lesson XXIX: The Town Pump
steps: New words: perpetuity (forever), municipality (a town), unadulterated (pure), rubicund (red-faced), replenish (to fill again)
Read the speech aloud as the Town Pump, in a booming, self-important voice
Narrate: who comes to drink at the pump, and what does it say to each?
questions: Which town officers does the pump claim to be like?
What does the pump call its water?
Which partner will help the pump 'reform the age'?
answers: Treasurer, overseer of the poor, fire chief, physician, constable, and town clerk
The unadulterated ale of father Adam
The cow (milk and water)
lessons.notes: By Nathaniel Hawthorne, from 'Twice-Told Tales.' A humorous temperance speech; gout was a painful disease linked with rich food and wine.

lessons.title: Lesson XXX: Good Night
steps: Read the poem aloud in a hushed voice, slowing on each 'Good night'
Copywork: one stanza of your choice
At bedtime, say your own good nights to things in your yard
questions: Which birds have gone quiet?
What creatures are still awake at night?
Who 'will sleep' at the end?
answers: The jay and the robin (and the crow dreams)
The bat, the fox, and the owl
Love and innocence
lessons.notes: Poem by Samuel Goodrich ('Peter Parley').

lessons.title: Lesson XXXI: An Old-Fashioned Girl
steps: New words: imposing (impressive), meteor (shooting star), blasé (bored with everything), invalid (a sickly person)
Read the passage aloud, giving Madam Shaw a slow old voice and Polly a fresh young one
Written narration: in a paragraph, describe Polly's visit to the Shaws
Discuss Madam Shaw's idea of what childhood should be
questions: Why was Polly glad when dinner was over?
How did Polly win over Madam Shaw?
How did Madam earn her first money?
answers: Tom stared at her, Madam peered at her, and Maud fussed; it was uncomfortable
She sang old songs for her
By sewing the best darn in her father's silk stockings, for a five-dollar prize
lessons.notes: From 'An Old-Fashioned Girl' by Louisa May Alcott, author of 'Little Women.' A good lead-in to the whole novel.

lessons.title: Lesson XXXII: My Mother's Hands
steps: Read the poem aloud with feeling
Copywork: "Such beautiful, beautiful hands!" and the two lines after it
Narrate: why does the writer find her mother's plain hands beautiful?
questions: Are the mother's hands white and small?
What did the hands do while the child played?
What does the writer hope for in the last stanza?
answers: No; they are aged and wrinkled
Kept working for the children
To hold her mother's hands again in heaven

lessons.title: Lesson XXXIII: The Discontented Pendulum
steps: New words: instituted (began), calculating (reckoning), harangue (a long speech), illustrate (to make clear), execute (to carry out)
Read the fable aloud, giving voices to the dial plate and the pendulum
Check the minute hand's arithmetic: how many seconds are in a day?
Narrate: how did the dial plate change the pendulum's mind?
questions: Why did the pendulum stop?
How many times does it tick in a day?
What did the farmer think when he saw the clock?
answers: It was tired of thinking about how many ticks it had ahead
That his watch had gained half an hour in the night
lessons.notes: By Jane Taylor (who wrote 'Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star'). The math: 60 × 60 × 24 = 86,400.

lessons.title: Lesson XXXIV: The Death of the Flowers
steps: New words: wailing (mourning), sear (withered), glade (an open space in a forest), unmeet (unfitting)
Read the poem aloud slowly, in a soft autumn voice
Memorize: the first four lines
Name the flowers in the poem in the order they die
questions: What month is it in the poem?
Which flowers last into autumn?
Who does the poet remember in the last stanza?
answers: November
The golden-rod, the aster, and the yellow sunflower
A beautiful young woman who died young (his sister)
lessons.notes: Poem by William Cullen Bryant, written in memory of his sister.

lessons.title: Lesson XXXV: The Thunderstorm
steps: New words: languor (dullness), predecessor (the one before), clamorously (noisily), defile (a narrow pass), rack (flying broken clouds)
Read the passage aloud, quietly at first, then with growing force as the storm breaks
Written narration: in a paragraph, describe a storm you remember, using two of Irving's words
questions: What river is Dolph sailing on?
What signs showed the storm was coming?
Why did the thunder seem so loud?
answers: The Hudson, through the Highlands
White clouds piling up, faint thunder, a dark ripple on the water, and birds flying to shelter
It echoed from mountain to mountain
lessons.notes: By Washington Irving, from 'Bracebridge Hall.' Find the Hudson Highlands on a map.

lessons.title: Lesson XXXVI: April Day
steps: New words: garnered (stored up), studs (buds), cleaving (splitting open), amber (golden yellow)
Read the poem aloud as gently as a spring rain
Copywork: "I could have half believed I heard / The leaves and blossoms growing."
Go outside after a rain and notice what has grown
questions: What sound did the poet listen to all day?
What did she half believe she heard?
What happened at the end of the rain?
answers: The steady rain
The leaves and blossoms growing
Golden light broke through, then one last shower fell
lessons.notes: Poem by Caroline Southey (Caroline Bowles).

lessons.title: Lesson XXXVII: The Tea Rose
steps: New words: ottoman (a backless padded seat), asylum (a place of refuge), bijou (a jewel), sentimental (overly full of feeling), yearns (longs)
Read the conversation aloud with two readers as Kate and Florence
Written narration: in a paragraph, give Florence's reasons for giving the rose to the Stephens family
questions: Who did Kate want Florence to give the rose to?
Who did Florence give it to instead?
What does Florence say about the beautiful things God makes?
answers: Mrs. Marshall, a wealthy friend with a greenhouse
Little Mary Stephens and her mother, a poor seamstress family
They are his gifts to everyone alike, rich or poor
lessons.notes: By Harriet Beecher Stowe (not named in the book). Kate's remarks about the poor show old class attitudes that the story itself argues against.

lessons.title: Lesson XXXVIII: The Cataract of Lodore
steps: New words: tarn (a small mountain lake), fell (a stony hill), gills (brooks), brawling (roaring), riving (splitting)
Read the poem aloud, speeding up as the water rushes; it is great practice for crisp '-ing' endings
Pick your favorite run of rhyming words and say it as fast and clearly as you can
Copywork: "Helter-skelter, / Hurry-skurry."
questions: Who asked the poet how the water comes down at Lodore?
Where does the stream rest before the falls?
Why does the poet call himself 'Laureate'?
answers: His little boy (and then his daughters)
In its own little lake
He was the official poet laureate of England
lessons.notes: Poem by Robert Southey, about a waterfall near his home in England's Lake District.

lessons.title: Lesson XXXIX: The Bobolink
steps: New words: varlet (a rascal), voluptuary (one who lives for pleasure), gourmand (a glutton), corpulent (fat), eschew (to avoid)
Read the essay aloud, cheerful in the first half and mock-serious in the second
Written narration: in a paragraph, tell the bobolink's 'career' from spring meadow to dinner table
Look up a picture of a bobolink in breeding plumage
questions: When is the bobolink happiest and most in song?
What two other names does he get as he flies south?
What moral does Irving draw for 'little birds and little boys'?
answers: From mid-May to mid-June, when the clover blooms
Reedbird and ricebird
Keep to refined, worthy pursuits and avoid greedy self-indulgence
lessons.notes: By Washington Irving. Shooting bobolinks for food was common then; today they are protected songbirds. Pairs well with the next poem.

lessons.title: Lesson XL: Robert of Lincoln
steps: Read the poem aloud, making the 'Bobolink, bobolink, spink, spank, spink' chorus bubble
Compare Bryant's bobolink with Irving's from the last lesson
Memorize: the first stanza
questions: How is Robert of Lincoln dressed?
How is his wife different from him?
Why is Robert 'sober with work' later in the summer?
answers: In a black 'wedding coat' with white shoulders and crest
She is quiet and plain brown, and sits patiently on the nest
He has six hungry nestlings to feed
lessons.notes: Poem by William Cullen Bryant.

lessons.title: Lesson XLI: Rebellion in Massachusetts State Prison
steps: New words: brigands (robbers), demeanor (behavior), parley (a talk with an enemy), expostulated (reasoned earnestly), intrepid (fearless)
Read the account aloud, letting the tension build toward the three minutes
Written narration: in a paragraph, compare the courage of the unarmed officer and of Major Wainright
questions: Why did the prisoners gather in the dining hall?
What did the mild officer carry into the hall?
How did Major Wainright end the rebellion without firing a shot?
answers: To stop three fellow prisoners from being whipped
Only his walking stick (a rattan)
He had the marines load and aim, then gave the prisoners three minutes to leave
lessons.notes: By J. T. Buckingham. Describes prison flogging and a tense armed standoff; the prisoners are described harshly.

lessons.title: Lesson XLII: Faithless Nelly Gray
steps: New words: devoirs (respects), scoff (a laughingstock), uniform (both 'consistent' and 'military dress'), blithe (merry)
Read the poem aloud and hunt for the puns: count them as you go
Explain three of the puns in your own words
questions: How did Ben Battle lose his legs?
What is the double meaning of 'laid down his arms'?
What is the pun in 'stand upon another footing'?
answers: A cannonball took them off
He put down his weapons, and he lost his limbs
His situation has changed, and he literally stands on different (wooden) feet
lessons.notes: Comic poem by Thomas Hood, full of puns. It ends with Ben hanging himself, told as a joke. Preview it, and you may want to skip it or discuss it with care.

lessons.title: Lesson XLIII: The Generous Russian Peasant
steps: New words: extol (to praise highly), annals (records), granary (a storehouse for grain), succor (help), superfluities (more than is needed)
Read the story aloud
Find the Volga River and Simbirsk on a map
Written narration: in a paragraph, tell how Flor Silin used his full granaries
questions: What was the 'Famine Year'?
What did Flor Silin do with his grain?
What did he tell his neighbors to do with the grain they tried to repay?
answers: A year of drought that ruined the harvests on the Lower Volga
Gave it to his starving neighbors and to anyone who asked
Share it with poor neighbors who still had nothing
lessons.notes: By Nikolai Karamzin, a Russian writer and historian. Old books use 'corn' for any grain.

lessons.title: Lesson XLIV: Forty Years Ago
steps: Read the poem aloud slowly, as an old man talking to his friend Tom
List what has changed at the old school and what is the same
Copywork: the last four lines of any stanza
questions: Where is the old schoolmaster now?
What did the speaker cut into the elm tree?
How many of the old class are still alive?
answers: Buried on the hill where they used to slide
Tom's name and his sweetheart's
Only the speaker and Tom
lessons.notes: A nostalgic song-poem. Ask a grandparent what has changed since they were in school.

lessons.title: Lesson XLV: Mrs. Caudle's Lecture
steps: New words: aggravating (irritating), vindictive (revengeful), paltry (petty)
Read the monologue aloud in Mrs. Caudle's voice, answering things Mr. Caudle never gets to say
Narrate: what is the whole quarrel about, and how does it grow?
questions: What started Mrs. Caudle's complaint?
What does she threaten to stop doing?
How does the lecture end?
answers: Mr. Caudle grumbled that a button was off his shirt
Sewing on his buttons
She accuses him of snoring
lessons.notes: By Douglas Jerrold, from 'Mrs. Caudle's Curtain Lectures' in Punch. A comic monologue that pokes fun at a nagging wife; an old-style joke.

lessons.title: Lesson XLVI: The Village Blacksmith
steps: Read the poem aloud with a steady, hammering rhythm
Memorize: the first two stanzas
Narrate: what lesson does the poet take from the blacksmith?
questions: Where does the smithy stand?
Why can the blacksmith 'look the whole world in the face'?
What makes him think of his wife in church?
answers: Under a spreading chestnut tree
He owes no one anything
His daughter's voice singing in the choir
lessons.notes: Poem by Henry Wadsworth Longfellow, one of the best-loved American poems.

lessons.title: Lesson XLVII: The Relief of Lucknow
steps: New words: siege (an army surrounding a place to force its surrender), slogan (a Highland war cry), pibroch (bagpipe music), sappers (soldiers who dig toward a fort), simultaneous (at the same moment)
Read the letter aloud, giving Jessie Brown's Scottish words their sound
Find Lucknow, India, on a map
Written narration: in a paragraph, tell how Jessie heard help coming before anyone else
questions: What did Jessie Brown hear?
Why did the others not believe her at first?
What tune did the pipers play at the banquet?
answers: The Highlanders' bagpipes and war cry
They could hear only the guns; their Lowland ears didn't catch the pipes
Auld Lang Syne
lessons.notes: From a letter to the London Times about the 1857 siege of Lucknow during the Indian Rebellion. It tells only the British side; historians doubt the Jessie Brown story, and Indians remember the uprising as a fight against British rule.

lessons.title: Lesson XLVIII: The Snowstorm
steps: New words: mazy (winding), hoar (grayish white), boon (a gift), askance (sideways), dire (dreadful)
Read the blank verse aloud, pausing by sense, not at line ends
Narrate: how does the snow affect the ox, the robin, the hare, and the sheep?
Copywork: "The cherished fields / Put on their winter robe of purest white."
questions: Which bird visits the house?
What does the robin do once it feels at home?
What does the poet urge shepherds to do?
answers: The redbreast (robin)
Pecks at the crumbs on the table
Feed and shelter their flocks, and watch for drifting snow
lessons.notes: From 'The Seasons' by James Thomson, a Scottish poet of the 1700s.

lessons.title: Lesson XLIX: Behind Time
steps: New words: collision (a crash), corps (a body of troops), remittances (money sent from a distance), ignominious (shameful), weal (well-being)
Read the essay aloud, pausing after each example
Written narration: in a paragraph, retell one of the four examples and add one of your own about being on time
questions: Why did the two trains crash?
Whose lateness, according to the essay, lost the battle of Waterloo?
Why was the condemned man hanged?
answers: An engineer was behind time
Marshal Grouchy's
The rider with his reprieve arrived five minutes too late
lessons.notes: Includes a train wreck and a hanging. The Waterloo claim simplifies history.

lessons.title: Lesson L: The Old Sampler
steps: New words: warder (a guard), antique (old), saffron (deep yellow), chapeau (a hat), supine (listless)
Read the poem aloud tenderly
Look at pictures of old samplers; if you sew, stitch your name and age
Narrate: what can we guess about Elizabeth's life from the chest?
questions: What did Elizabeth stitch on her sampler?
Which war does the rusty sword come from?
What sorrow did Elizabeth suffer later?
answers: "Elizabeth, Aged Nine," inside a wreath of berry and vine
The American Revolution (from Lexington to Yorktown)
The man who wore the plumed hat was killed by a sword thrust
lessons.notes: Poem by Margaret E. Sangster. A sampler is a piece of practice needlework.

lessons.title: Lesson LI: The Goodness of God
steps: New words: habitation (dwelling), refuge (shelter), cony (a small rock-dwelling animal)
Read the passages aloud reverently
Make a list of all the creatures the psalm names
Copywork: "O Lord, how manifold are thy works!"
questions: What does the psalm say God uses as his chariot?
Where does the stork make her home?
What does man do when the sun rises?
answers: The clouds
In the fir trees
Goes out to his work until evening
lessons.notes: Mostly from Psalm 104, with lines from Psalms 107 and 105.

lessons.title: Lesson LII: My Mother
steps: Read the poem aloud quietly
Copywork: "Whispering, 'God will keep my child.'"
Narrate: how does the speaker feel about the trouble he caused his mother?
questions: What did the mother whisper after praying?
What is the mother compared to now?
What does the speaker promise in the last stanza?
answers: "God will keep my child."
A faded autumn leaf
To share her troubles, watch beside her, and pray with her

lessons.title: Lesson LIII: The Hour of Prayer
steps: Read the poem aloud, pausing on the refrain 'Lift the heart, and bend the knee'
List everyone the poem calls to prayer
Memorize: the first stanza
questions: What time of day is the poem set?
Name three people far from home whom the poet calls to pray.
What one thing do the joyful and the sorrowful all see?
answers: Sunset, as evening falls
The traveler, the captive, and the sailor (also the mourner)
Heaven's first star
lessons.notes: Poem by Felicia Hemans.

lessons.title: Lesson LIV: The Will
steps: New words: reprobate (a person gone bad), deceased (dead), convened (gathered), chaise (a light two-wheeled carriage), profligate (a shameless spendthrift)
Read the play aloud with four readers (or one reader doing voices), letting the Squire pause slowly with his spectacles
Narrate: how did the two greedy cousins change as the will was read?
questions: Why did Swipes and Currie expect to inherit?
What two words in the will changed everything?
Why were the cousins released from being trustees at the end?
answers: They heard the old lady had cut off her nephew Frank
"In trust"
The will was three years old, so Frank was already twenty-one
lessons.notes: A short comic play. Legal phrases like 'will and testament' pair words of the same meaning, as the book's note explains.

lessons.title: Lesson LV: The Nose and the Eyes
steps: New words: argued (reasoned), discerning (telling things apart), behalf (on the side of), decreed (ordered by a judge)
Read the poem aloud as a pompous courtroom speech
Narrate: what were the lawyer's arguments for the Nose?
Discuss what is silly about the judge's decision
questions: What were the Nose and the Eyes arguing about?
Who were the lawyer and the judge?
What did the judge decide?
answers: Which of them the spectacles belong to
Tongue was the lawyer and Ear was the judge
Whenever the Nose wears the spectacles, the Eyes must be shut
lessons.notes: Comic poem by William Cowper, poking fun at lawyers and courts.

lessons.title: Lesson LVI: An Iceberg
steps: New words: serenity (calm), exquisite (very fine), monochromist (one who paints in one color), polychroic (many-colored), obliquely (slantwise)
Read the passage aloud, building to the great roll of the iceberg
Written narration: in a paragraph, describe the 'polar bear' piece of ice and how the waves attacked it
Float an ice cube in a glass and see how much is under water
questions: What did the small piece of floating ice look like?
What happened to the big iceberg while the travelers watched?
How much of an iceberg is above water, according to the note?
answers: A huge polar bear
It cracked and rolled over in the water
About one eighth
lessons.notes: By Louis Legrand Noble, from 'After Icebergs with a Painter' (a voyage with the painter Frederic Church). Scientists today usually say about one tenth of an iceberg shows above water.

lessons.title: Lesson LVII: About Quail
steps: New words: aquatic (living in or near water), cupidity (greed), tussock (a tuft of grass), cradler (a reaper with a grain cradle), devious (winding)
Read the essay aloud warmly
Written narration: in a paragraph, describe how a mother quail protects her chicks
Listen online to a bobwhite quail's call
questions: How is the quail different from the birds that migrate?
What does the mother quail do when someone startles her family?
What does the male quail call?
answers: He stays home all year, near the farm where he was born
Pretends to be hurt and leads the intruder away, then flies back to her chicks
"Bob White!"
lessons.notes: By William Post Hawes, a sportsman writer. Boreas was the Greek north wind.

lessons.title: Lesson LVIII: The Blue and the Gray
steps: Read the poem aloud slowly, varying the last lines of each stanza
Learn what 'the Blue' and 'the Gray' mean
Memorize: the last stanza
Narrate: what generous deed does the poem honor?
questions: Who are 'the Blue' and 'the Gray'?
What did the mourners bring to the graves?
What does the poem hope for in the last stanza?
answers: Union and Confederate soldiers of the Civil War
Flowers, for friend and foe alike
That anger is banished forever and both sides are mourned with love
lessons.notes: By Francis Miles Finch (1867), honoring women in Columbus, Mississippi, who decorated both Union and Confederate graves. A good place to talk about the Civil War and Memorial Day.

lessons.title: Lesson LIX: The Machinist's Return
steps: New words: maneuvers (movements), portmanteau (a traveling bag), confidant (one you tell secrets to), mortgaged (pledged for a debt), pantomime (acting without words)
Read the story aloud, enjoying the nervous traveler
Written narration: in a paragraph, tell the machinist's story in his own voice
questions: Why was the stranger so excited?
Who believed in his invention when no one else did?
How did his wife support the family while he was away?
answers: He was coming home rich after three years in Europe, earlier than expected
His wife
By sewing shirts for thirteen cents apiece
lessons.notes: From a newspaper letter. £50,000 was a huge fortune then.

lessons.title: Lesson LX: Make Way for Liberty
steps: New words: phalanx (soldiers in close ranks), rampart (a defensive wall), impregnable (unbreakable), annihilates (destroys), breach (a gap)
Read the poem aloud with rising force, shouting the refrain
Narrate: how did Arnold Winkelried open the Austrian line?
questions: What does the poem compare the Austrian army to?
What did Winkelried do?
Where and when did this battle happen?
answers: A living wall and a human wood
Gathered the enemy spears into his own body, opening a gap for his comrades
At Sempach, Switzerland, in 1386
lessons.notes: Poem by James Montgomery about a Swiss hero. Includes a soldier's death in battle.

lessons.title: Lesson LXI: The English Skylark
steps: New words: ecstasy (great joy), axiom (a self-evident truth), gyrations (circling motions), undulating (rising and falling like waves), hamlet (a small village)
Read the passage aloud lightly, letting the sentences soar
Copywork: "It mounts up like a human aspiration."
Listen to a recording of a skylark
questions: What does the skylark look like on the ground?
How is its flight different from an eagle's?
How far away can its song be heard?
answers: Plain, shy, and silent
It rises straight up, not in circles
Nearly a mile
lessons.notes: By Elihu Burritt, 'the learned blacksmith,' who taught himself many languages.

lessons.title: Lesson LXII: How Sleep the Brave
steps: Read the short poem aloud slowly and reverently
Memorize: the whole poem (12 lines)
Talk about who the 'brave' are and how they are honored
questions: Who are 'the brave' in the poem?
Who comes as a gray pilgrim to bless their graves?
Who will dwell there like a weeping hermit?
answers: Soldiers who died for their country
Honor
Freedom
lessons.notes: Ode by William Collins (1746), a fine poem for Memorial Day or Veterans Day.

lessons.title: Lesson LXIII: The Rainbow
steps: Read the poem aloud thoughtfully
Copywork: the last stanza
Narrate: what does the rainbow teach about joy and grief?
questions: Where was the storm an hour ago?
According to the poem, when will grief become joy?
answers: Right where the poet was (now the rainbow is there)
When the 'holiest ray,' the light of heaven, falls on it
lessons.notes: Poem by John Keble, from a book of religious verse.

lessons.title: Lesson LXIV: Supposed Speech of John Adams
steps: New words: reconciliation (making peace again), colleague (a fellow officer), proscribed (outlawed), predestined (decided beforehand), clemency (mercy)
Read the speech aloud as an orator, building to 'Independence forever'
Written narration: in a paragraph, give three of Adams's reasons for declaring independence now
Memorize: the opening sentence, 'Sink or swim, live or die...'
questions: Who actually wrote this speech?
Why does Adams say Hancock and Samuel Adams are already outlaws?
How does he predict future Americans will celebrate the day?
answers: Daniel Webster, imagining what Adams might have said
The British had excluded them from any pardon
With thanksgiving, festivity, bonfires, and illuminations
lessons.notes: Daniel Webster wrote this in 1826 as part of a eulogy for Adams and Jefferson; it isn't Adams's real speech. Read it near the Fourth of July.

lessons.title: Lesson LXV: The Rising
steps: New words: boreal (northern), yeoman (a farmer who owns land), manor (an estate), theme (a subject), guise (appearance)
Read the poem aloud with growing energy, ringing out the 'WAR! WAR! WAR!'
Narrate: what happened in the church at Berkley Manor?
questions: What news came 'out of the North'?
What did the women do to help?
What did the pastor reveal under his gown?
answers: The fighting at Lexington and Concord
Poured lead into molds to make bullets
A soldier's uniform; he called for volunteers and a hundred men enlisted
lessons.notes: From 'The Wagoner of the Alleghanies' by Thomas Buchanan Read, about Pastor Peter Muhlenberg, who became a Revolutionary general.

lessons.title: Lesson LXVI: Control Your Temper
steps: New words: culture (training), disciplined (trained), deference (respect), reprimanded (scolded), superannuated (weakened by age)
Read the lesson aloud
Written narration: in a paragraph, tell the two stories about Roger Sherman and what they show
Talk about one thing that tries your temper and how you could answer it calmly
questions: What did Roger Sherman do when a student flashed sunlight in his eyes?
Why did Sherman's mother box his ear?
Who was Roger Sherman?
answers: He quietly closed the window blind
Because he tapped his own child's ear during family prayers
A shoemaker who became a judge, congressman, and signer of the Declaration of Independence
lessons.notes: By Dr. John Todd. Mentions caring for 'deranged people' (an old term for mental illness).

lessons.title: Lesson LXVII: William Tell (Part 1)
steps: New words: comeliness (gracefulness), avalanche (a mass of snow sliding down a mountain), fledgling (a young bird), caitiff (a mean villain), thralldom (slavery)
Read the scene aloud as a play, with readers for Tell, Gesler, Sarnem, and Albert
Narrate: how did Gesler find out that Albert was Tell's son, and what cruel test did he set?
questions: Why did Albert pretend not to know his father?
What does Tell say vengeance cannot take away?
What does Gesler order Tell to do?
answers: To keep from sharing his father's death
His honor, good name, and virtue
Shoot an apple off his son's head from a hundred paces
lessons.notes: From the play 'William Tell' by James Sheridan Knowles. Tell is a Swiss legend set in 1307. The next lesson finishes the story.

lessons.title: Lesson LXVIII: William Tell (Concluded)
steps: New words: accords (grants), issue (outcome), stanch (sound and true), shaft (the stem of an arrow), quiver (a case for arrows)
Read the scene aloud as a play, slowly building to the shot
Written narration: in a paragraph, tell how Tell prepared for the shot and why he hid the second arrow
questions: Why did Tell want the sun at his back?
Why did he break and throw away the arrows the soldier gave him?
What was the hidden arrow for?
answers: So it would shine on the target, not in his eyes
They were bent, jagged, or too heavy for such an aim
To kill Gesler if he had killed his son
lessons.notes: The book's note tells the rest of the legend: Tell escaped and later shot Gesler. Ending a tyrant's life is presented as heroic; worth a short talk.

lessons.title: Lesson LXIX: The Crazy Engineer
steps: New words: competent (qualified), juncture (a critical moment), remonstrate (to protest), apprehend (to fear), tender (the fuel car behind a locomotive)
Read the story aloud, letting the speed and danger grow
Find Danzig (Gdańsk) and the Vistula River on a map
Written narration: in a paragraph, tell how the train was saved
questions: Why did the conductor need a new engineer?
Who was Martin Kroller really?
How was Kroller stopped?
answers: His engineer had been badly hurt
A madman escaped from the hospital at Stettin, obsessed with an engine to reach the moon
A German student knocked the pistol from his hand and struck him with a stick of wood
lessons.notes: An exciting story set in old Prussia (now Poland). Uses dated words like 'crazy' and 'maniac' for mental illness, and includes a pistol and a near-crash.

lessons.title: Lesson LXX: The Heritage
steps: New words: heritage (what is inherited), sated (overfull), hinds (farm workers), adjudged (decided), benign (wholesome)
Read the poem aloud, contrasting the rich man's son and the poor man's son
Memorize: the fourth stanza, 'What doth the poor man's son inherit?'
Narrate: what does the poet say both sons inherit in the end?
questions: Name two cares the rich man's son inherits.
What does the poor man's son inherit?
What does the poet advise the rich man's son to do?
answers: The bank may break, the factory may burn, his shares may fail; he has soft hands that can't earn a living
Strong muscles, a hardy spirit, contentment in work, patience, and courage
Do large charity, the best crop from his lands
lessons.notes: Poem by James Russell Lowell. 'To hold in fee' means to own as an inheritance.

lessons.title: Lesson LXXI: No Excellence Without Labor
steps: New words: architects (builders), mediocrity (ordinary ability), absolve (to release), fiat (a decree), prowess (bravery)
Read the essay aloud like a speech
Written narration: in a paragraph, explain Wirt's comparison of the genius and the plodder, and say whether you agree
questions: Who does Wirt say must do most of a person's education?
What often happens to the lazy genius and the hardworking ordinary student?
What bird and mountain does he use for true genius?
answers: The person himself
The genius sinks into poverty while the plodder rises to success
The condor soaring from Chimborazo
lessons.notes: By William Wirt, U.S. Attorney General. Find Chimborazo in Ecuador on a map. Quotes Shakespeare's 'Henry IV, Part 1.'

lessons.title: Lesson LXXII: The Old House Clock
steps: Read the poem aloud, ticking out the rhythm of the refrain
Compare the three messages the clock gives: at night, at dawn, and at the end of life
Copywork: the 'Tick! tick!' lines from the first stanza
questions: What does the clock warn at ten o'clock?
What does it say at five in the morning?
What 'morning' does the last stanza mean?
answers: Go to bed, or you'll never rise early
Get up, for no one has health or wealth without rising early
The heavenly morning after death

lessons.title: Lesson LXXIII: The Examination
steps: New words: tempered (hardened), compact (dense), porous (full of tiny holes), evaporated (passed off as vapor), apparatus (equipment for experiments)
Read the scene aloud, giving Bunker a shrewd country voice
Try Locke's demonstration: put a heavy object in a cup of water and watch the water rise
Narrate: how did Locke teach the boy why smoke rises?
questions: Why does breath disappear faster from a good knife, according to Bunker?
What does Bunker say is half the battle for a teacher?
Why does smoke go up the chimney?
answers: Its steel is more compact, with smaller pores
Being able to teach others to think
Heavier cold air settles and pushes the warm air (with the smoke) upward
lessons.notes: From 'Locke Amsden, the Schoolmaster' by Daniel Pierce Thompson. Bunker's theories about the knife and frozen paths are clever but not modern science; the lesson on teaching is the point.

lessons.title: Lesson LXXIV: The Isle of Long Ago
steps: New words: realm (region), rhythm (a flowing beat), surge (a great swell of water), mirage (an illusion of things floating in the air), aye (always)
Read the poem aloud dreamily, feeling its rocking rhythm
Narrate: what 'treasures' are buried on the Isle of Long Ago?
questions: What is time compared to in the poem?
What is the Isle of Long Ago?
Name two things kept on the isle.
answers: A river flowing into the ocean of years
Our memories of the past and of loved ones gone
Locks of hair, unsung songs, a child's prayer, broken rings, a harp without strings
lessons.notes: Poem by Benjamin Franklin Taylor, about memory and loss.

lessons.title: Lesson LXXV: The Boston Massacre
steps: New words: indiscriminately (without distinction), ensued (followed), ensign (a junior officer), brandishing (waving), warrant (an order to arrest)
Read the account aloud
Find King Street (now State Street) on a map of Boston
Written narration: in a paragraph, tell how the trouble began and how it ended
questions: What date did the Boston Massacre happen?
Who warned Captain Preston to take his men back?
How did the townspeople respond the next day?
answers: March 5, 1770
Henry Knox
They stood calm and demanded justice by law; Preston and his soldiers were arrested
lessons.notes: From George Bancroft's 'History of the United States,' which tells the story strongly from the colonists' side. John Adams later defended the soldiers in court and most were acquitted. Crispus Attucks, killed here, was a man of African and Native American descent.

lessons.title: Lesson LXXVI: Death of the Beautiful
steps: Read the short poem aloud gently
Copywork: the last stanza
Talk about the comfort the poet offers
questions: What does the poet say happens too soon to earth's fairest flowers?
Why does she say we should dry our tears?
answers: They decay
The lovely ones who die came to raise our hearts to heaven and go to call us there
lessons.notes: Poem by Eliza Lee Follen, about the death of the young. Pair it with the next short poem for one sitting if you like.

lessons.title: Lesson LXXVII: Snow Falling
steps: New words: wold (open country), spectral (ghostly), banished (driven away)
Read the two stanzas aloud softly
Memorize: the whole poem (8 lines)
Watch snow (or picture it) and write one sentence comparing it to something
questions: What does the snow look like on the trees?
What does the poet imagine the snowflakes are?
answers: Ghostly blossoms
Flowers banished from a garden in heaven
lessons.notes: Poem by John James Piatt.

lessons.title: Lesson LXXVIII: Squeers's Method
steps: New words: fustian (a coarse cotton cloth), grotesque (absurd), corporeal (bodily), temporary (for the time being), disconcerted (flustered)
Read the scene aloud, giving Squeers a blustering voice
Written narration: in a paragraph, describe Dotheboys Hall and explain what is wrong with Squeers's 'practical mode of teaching'
questions: What did Mrs. Squeers give the boys before breakfast?
Where was the first boy of the spelling class?
What is Squeers really using his 'system' for?
answers: Brimstone and treacle, from a huge wooden spoon
Cleaning the back parlor window
To make the boys do his chores
lessons.notes: From 'Nicholas Nickleby' by Charles Dickens, which exposed cruel boarding schools in Yorkshire. Describes mistreated and disabled children.

lessons.title: Lesson LXXIX: The Gift of Empty Hands
steps: New words: doomed (condemned), charmed (enchanted), weird (magical), quick (alive), mute (silent)
Read the poem aloud like a fairy tale
Narrate: why did the king value the empty, scarred hands more?
questions: What did the two princes promise the king?
How did one prince get his treasures so easily?
What did the king say about true treasure?
answers: To bring him fair gifts if he spared their lives
They fell or flew to him without any struggle
It is not lightly won; the scars of honest effort are worth more
lessons.notes: Poem by Sarah Morgan Bryan Piatt.

lessons.title: Lesson LXXX: Capturing the Wild Horse
steps: New words: diversified (varied), ruminating (chewing the cud), lariat (a rope with a noose), covert (a hiding place), mercurial (lively, changeable)
Read the account aloud, quick and lively in the chase
Draw a diagram of the 'ringing the wild horse' plan
Written narration: in a paragraph, tell how the plan was supposed to work and how Tonish spoiled it
questions: What is 'ringing the wild horse'?
Who spoiled the plan?
What horses did the hunters catch?
answers: Surrounding a herd with a big ring of riders and running them until they tire
Tonish, the excitable little Frenchman
A black mare and a cream-colored colt
lessons.notes: From Washington Irving's 'A Tour on the Prairies' (1835), in what is now Oklahoma. The guides are called 'half-breeds,' a term now considered offensive for people of mixed Native and European descent.

lessons.title: Lesson LXXXI: Sowing and Reaping
steps: Read the poem aloud earnestly
Memorize: the first stanza
Talk about what kinds of 'seed' a person can sow besides grain
questions: When does the poem say to wait for the harvest?
Should the sower care who reaps the harvest?
What does the last stanza promise?
answers: Till autumn
No; sow today even if someone else reaps it
You will reap in joy what you sowed in tears
lessons.notes: Poem by Adelaide Anne Procter. Echoes Psalm 126:5.

lessons.title: Lesson LXXXII: Taking Comfort
steps: New words: transient (brief), picturesque (pretty as a picture), panorama (a wide view), reverie (a daydream), malediction (a curse)
Read the sketch aloud: peaceful in the first half, then sad
Written narration: in a paragraph, contrast the autumn scene with the man lying in the dirt
questions: Where was the writer walking?
What did the little boy ask the man on the ground?
What did the man answer?
answers: Along the Merrimack River near Lowell, Massachusetts
What ails you? Why do you lie there?
"I'm taking comfort"
lessons.notes: By John Greenleaf Whittier. A temperance sketch about a drunken man; a chance to talk about addiction.

lessons.title: Lesson LXXXIII: Calling the Roll
steps: Read the poem aloud slowly; let a second reader call out the names and answer 'Here!'
Narrate: what happened to each soldier whose name was called?
Talk about why the poet ends with a number
questions: What happened when Cyrus Drew's name was called?
How did Herbert Cline answer?
How many men answered 'here' at the end?
answers: No one answered; he had fallen
Two soldiers carried him in, wounded, to answer his name
Twenty out of a hundred
lessons.notes: Civil War poem by N. G. Shepherd. Vivid images of battle and death.

lessons.title: Lesson LXXXIV: Turtle Soup
steps: New words: aft (toward the back of a ship), unctuous (rich and fatty), binnacle (the box holding a ship's compass), galley (a ship's kitchen), tureen (a large soup bowl)
Read the story aloud, enjoying the narrator's hungry daydream
Written narration: in a paragraph, tell what happened to the turtle soup and why the narrator laughed
questions: Why was the turtle saved until near the end of the voyage?
Why did the ship lurch?
What did the passengers eat for dinner instead?
answers: It wouldn't spoil, so the other animals were eaten first
The narrator was daydreaming about the soup and let the wheel slip
Cold ham
lessons.notes: By Charles F. Briggs, from 'Working a Passage.' Ships' time: four bells here means 2 o'clock.

lessons.title: Lesson LXXXV: The Best Kind of Revenge
steps: New words: scurrilous (insulting and coarse), libeler (one who prints lies about another), audacity (boldness), delinquent (an offender), stint (to cut short)
Read the story aloud, building to the surprise when Mr. Grant signs
Written narration: in a paragraph, explain what 'the best kind of revenge' is
questions: What had the warehouseman done to the Grant Brothers?
Why did he need their signature?
What did William Grant give him besides his signature?
answers: Published a pamphlet mocking them
He was bankrupt and needed all his creditors to sign his certificate to do business again
A ten-pound note for his family
lessons.notes: The Grant brothers of Manchester were the models for the kind Cheeryble brothers in Dickens's 'Nicholas Nickleby.'

lessons.title: Lesson LXXXVI: The Soldier of the Rhine
steps: New words: legion (a division of an army), dearth (lack), ebbed (flowed away), coquetry (flirting), yore (old times)
Read the poem aloud with feeling, slowing on each line about Bingen
Find Bingen on the Rhine River in Germany on a map
Narrate: what messages did the soldier send home?
questions: Where was the soldier dying?
What did he keep when his father died?
What did he dream of the night before?
answers: In Algiers, far from home
His father's sword
Walking with the girl he loved on the vine-clad hills of Bingen
lessons.notes: Poem ('Bingen on the Rhine') by Caroline Norton. A soldier's death in battle.

lessons.title: Lesson LXXXVII: The Winged Worshipers
steps: New words: penance (suffering for sin), lays (songs), choir (a group of singers), consecrated (set apart for God), trackless (without a path)
Read the poem aloud lightly
Copywork: one stanza of your choice
Narrate: what does the poet wish the birds could teach him?
questions: Who are the 'winged worshipers'?
Why don't the birds need to pray, according to the poet?
What does the poet wish he could do?
answers: Two swallows that flew into church during the service
They have no sins to be forgiven
Fly up with them to soar through the light and praise God
lessons.notes: Poem by Charles Sprague.

lessons.title: Lesson LXXXVIII: The Peevish Wife
steps: New words: irony (saying the opposite of what you mean), derision (mocking laughter), incompatible (unable to exist together)
Read the dialogue with two readers, keeping Mr. Bolingbroke patient and Mrs. Bolingbroke cross
Narrate: how does Mrs. Bolingbroke twist everything her husband says?
questions: What news was in the paper?
Why was Mrs. Bolingbroke upset that her husband told her the first marriage?
Why does she finally decide to visit Mrs. Granby?
answers: Two friends had married: Mrs. Nettleby and Mr. Granby
It spoiled the pleasure of being surprised
Out of curiosity, to see if she is really Emma Cooke
lessons.notes: By Maria Edgeworth. A comic sketch of a quarrelsome mood; a good chance to talk about being peevish.

lessons.title: Lesson LXXXIX: The Rainy Day
steps: Read the poem aloud, gloomy in the first two stanzas and hopeful in the third
Memorize: the whole poem (15 lines)
Narrate: how does the poet compare the weather to his life?
questions: What clings to the moldering wall?
What does the poet tell his sad heart in the last stanza?
answers: The vine
Stop complaining; the sun still shines behind the clouds, and into each life some rain must fall
lessons.notes: Poem by Henry Wadsworth Longfellow. Pairs well with the next poem for one sitting.

lessons.title: Lesson XC: Break, Break, Break
steps: Read the poem aloud slowly, letting the 'Break, break, break' sound like waves
Memorize: the whole poem (16 lines)
Talk about why the happy people in stanza 2 make the poet sadder
questions: Who is playing and singing by the sea?
What does the poet long for in the third stanza?
answers: A fisherman's boy and his sister, and a sailor lad
The touch of a vanished hand and the sound of a voice that is still
lessons.notes: Poem by Alfred Tennyson, written after his dear friend Arthur Hallam died young.

lessons.title: Lesson XCI: Transportation and Planting of Seeds
steps: New words: membrane (a thin tissue), propagation (reproduction), deciduous (losing leaves in fall), germinating (sprouting), disseminating (scattering)
Read the essay aloud, a section at a time
Written narration: in a paragraph, explain three ways seeds travel, according to Thoreau
Nature walk: look for pine seeds, acorn caps, or squirrel diggings
questions: How do pine seeds travel?
What do squirrels do with nuts that helps forests grow?
What bird does Thoreau say could replant all the cleared lands?
answers: On a thin wing the wind carries
They bury them or drop them in open land, where some sprout
The jay
lessons.notes: By Henry David Thoreau, from 'The Succession of Forest Trees.' The American chestnut trees he gathered from were later wiped out by blight.

lessons.title: Lesson XCII: Spring Again
steps: Read the poem aloud, wintry at first, then growing warm and glad
Memorize: the seventh stanza, 'Frost-locked, storm-beaten, and lonely...'
Narrate: what signs of coming spring does the poet notice on her island?
questions: Where is the poet standing?
What still lies in the hollows?
What tidings does the bleak rock hear?
answers: On a high point of her rocky island, looking at sea and land
Snow
"There shall be spring again!"
lessons.notes: Poem by Celia Thaxter, who grew up in a lighthouse on the Isles of Shoals off New Hampshire.

lessons.title: Lesson XCIII: Religion the Only Basis of Society
steps: New words: community (society), diffusion (spreading), perpetrator (one who commits a crime), extinction (ending), atheism (disbelief in God)
Read the essay aloud as a sermon
Written narration: in a paragraph, sum up Channing's argument and say what you think of it
questions: Why does Channing say religion is not just a private matter?
What does he say would happen to society if all belief in God were erased?
What does he compare trusting human laws alone to?
answers: It supports the virtues and principles society rests on
Selfishness would rule and society would fall into ruin
Hoping torches could light the world if the sun went out
lessons.notes: By William Ellery Channing, a Boston minister. A persuasive essay; older students can discuss it in light of your family's faith.

lessons.title: Lesson XCIV: Rock Me to Sleep
steps: Read the poem aloud softly, with the refrain like a lullaby
Copywork: the first two lines
Narrate: why does the speaker wish to be a child again?
questions: Whom is the speaker calling to?
What is she weary of?
What does she remember about her mother's hair?
answers: Her mother, who has died
Toil and tears, and sowing for others to reap
It was brown, touched with gold, and fell over her forehead
lessons.notes: By Elizabeth Akers Allen. The book notes that five different people falsely claimed to have written it.

lessons.title: Lesson XCV: Man and the Inferior Animals
steps: New words: distinction (a difference), implements (tools), medicinal (healing), endowed (gifted), rectified (corrected)
Read the essay aloud
Written narration: in a paragraph, explain the three differences between people and animals given in the essay
Discuss whether anything you know about animals (tool use, learning) challenges the essay
questions: What is the first difference between man and animals?
Why does the author say animals don't make mistakes?
How does she show that animals make no improvements?
answers: Man needs tools; animals use what nature gave them
They follow instinct, which is always perfect
A swallow's nest today is no better than one built in Noah's ark
lessons.notes: By Jane Taylor. Uses 'savage' for early peoples. Modern science has found animals that use tools and learn, a good topic for discussion.

lessons.title: Lesson XCVI: The Blind Men and the Elephant
steps: Read the poem aloud with a different voice for each blind man
Act it out: blindfold family members and let them describe an object by touch
Memorize: the first and last stanzas
Narrate: what is the poem's lesson?
questions: What did the man who felt the elephant's side think it was like?
What did the man holding the trunk say?
Why were all six both right and wrong?
answers: A wall
A snake
Each knew one part truly, but none understood the whole animal
lessons.notes: Poem by John Godfrey Saxe, retelling an old fable from India.

lessons.title: Lesson XCVII: A Home Scene
steps: New words: inexorable (unchangeable), wonted (usual), admonition (gentle warning), ponderous (very heavy), vague (unclear)
Read the passage aloud slowly, as a remembered evening
Written narration: in a paragraph, describe your own home on an ordinary evening, the way Mitchell does
questions: What does the boy find in the family Bible?
Who was Charlie?
What does the mother tell the boy as twilight deepens?
answers: The family record of births, marriages, and deaths
His little brother, who died at four
That she cannot be with him long, and he must learn to face the world on his own
lessons.notes: From 'Dream Life' by Donald Grant Mitchell ('Ik Marvel'). Mentions a child's death.

lessons.title: Lesson XCVIII: The Light of Other Days
steps: Read the song-poem aloud gently (try listening to it sung)
Memorize: the first stanza
Narrate: what is the 'light of other days'?
questions: When does memory bring back the light of other days?
What does the poet compare his lost friends to?
How does he feel, like someone in a deserted banquet hall?
answers: At night, before he falls asleep
Leaves falling in winter
Alone, with all the lights and guests gone
lessons.notes: Poem ('Oft in the Stilly Night') by Thomas Moore, from his Irish songs.

lessons.title: Lesson XCIX: A Chase in the English Channel
steps: New words: frigate (a warship), equipage (equipment), artifice (a clever trick), broadside (all of one side's guns firing at once), manifest (plain to see)
Read the passage aloud with energy, shouting Griffith's and the Pilot's orders
Written narration: in a paragraph, tell how the Pilot saved the American ship
questions: Why were Griffith and the Pilot worried during the battle?
What danger did Merry report?
How did the danger turn into their salvation?
answers: The English ship was their equal and the big ninety-gun ship was catching up
Breakers: they were running onto shoals
The Pilot steered them through the narrow channels, where the enemy couldn't follow
lessons.notes: From 'The Pilot' by James Fenimore Cooper. The mysterious Pilot is based on John Paul Jones of the Revolutionary navy. Sea battle with men killed.

lessons.title: Lesson C: Burial of Sir John Moore
steps: New words: martial (military), upbraid (to scold), reck (to care), random (without aim)
Read the poem aloud solemnly, at a slow march
Memorize: the first two stanzas
Find Corunna (A Coruña), Spain, on a map
questions: When and how was Sir John Moore buried?
What did they wrap him in?
Why did the soldiers have to hurry?
answers: Quickly, at midnight, by lantern light, without drums or a coffin
His soldier's cloak
The enemy was near and they had to leave by sea
lessons.notes: Poem by Charles Wolfe about a British general killed at Corunna in 1809 fighting Napoleon's army.

lessons.title: Lesson CI: Little Victories
steps: New words: afflicted (deeply troubled), reckoned (counted on), composer (one who writes music), orchestra (a group of musicians), dejected (discouraged)
Read the story aloud, with two readers for Hugh and his mother
Written narration: in a paragraph, explain what Hugh's mother means by 'little victories'
questions: Why was Hugh so upset?
Which two famous men did his mother tell him about?
What good things did his mother say might come from his lameness?
answers: He had lost his leg and could never be a soldier or sailor or go round the world
Huber, the blind naturalist, and Beethoven, the deaf composer
He would read more, be a better scholar, be more loved, and love God more
lessons.notes: By Harriet Martineau, from 'The Crofton Boys.' Hugh has had a leg amputated; the story describes 'phantom limb' feelings honestly and kindly.

lessons.title: Lesson CII: The Character of a Happy Life
steps: Read the poem aloud slowly, one stanza at a time
Make a list of what the happy man has and what he is free from
Memorize: the last stanza, 'This man is freed from servile bands...'
questions: What is the happy man's armor?
How does he spend a 'harmless day'?
What does the last line say he has, though he has nothing?
answers: His honest thought
With a religious book or a friend
All
lessons.notes: Poem by Sir Henry Wotton (around 1614). Some words are old: 'servile bands' means the chains of a servant.

lessons.title: Lesson CIII: The Art of Discouragement
steps: New words: designated (named), yam (a starchy root), impaled (stuck on a stake), dilate (to talk at length), projector (one who plans a project)
Read the essay aloud, enjoying the imaginary 'cold-water pourer' talking to the inventor of the wheel
Written narration: in a paragraph, give the reasons Helps says people discourage others
Talk about a time you were discouraged, or encouraged, about a new idea
questions: What does Helps's friend call people who discourage new ideas?
Name two arguments the 'friend' gave against the wheel.
Why is it 'safe' to predict failure?
answers: Cold-water pourers
People got along fine without it; it may be irreligious; it can't go uphill; you'll neglect your yams; it will ruin the burden carriers
Hardly anything succeeds at first exactly as planned
lessons.notes: By Arthur Helps. Includes a mention of a man being executed for inventing flint and steel, in a joking story.

lessons.title: Lesson CIV: The Mariner's Dream
steps: New words: hammock (a hanging bed), transport (great joy), impearled (decked with pearls), 'larums (alarms), dirge (funeral music)
Read the poem aloud: soft and happy for the dream, loud and fast for the storm
Narrate: what did the sailor boy dream, and what woke him?
questions: What did the sailor boy dream about?
What woke him?
Where does the poem say he will lie?
answers: Coming home to his parents and the girl he loved
Lightning, thunder, and a storm wrecking the ship
Deep in the sea, with coral growing around his bones
