lessons.notes: Poem by William Dimond. Ends with the boy drowning; old ideas about amber being made in the sea are poetic, not scientific.

lessons.title: Lesson CV: The Passenger Pigeon
steps: New words: aerial (in the air), anon (soon), mast (nuts and acorns on the forest floor), rendezvous (a meeting place), perambulate (to walk through)
Read the account aloud
Written narration: in a paragraph, describe the flocks Audubon saw, then add what happened to the passenger pigeon later
Look up a painting of passenger pigeons by Audubon
questions: How many flocks did Audubon count in twenty-one minutes?
What happened to the trees at the roosting place?
How far away could the noise of the roost be heard?
answers: Many large trees and branches broke under the weight of the birds
Three miles
lessons.notes: By John James Audubon. Passenger pigeons were hunted to extinction; the last one, Martha, died at the Cincinnati Zoo on September 1, 1914. Includes mass killing of birds; a powerful lesson in conservation.

lessons.title: Lesson CVI: The Country Life
steps: Read the poem aloud thoughtfully
Narrate: where does the poet live now, and where would he rather be?
Copywork: "Well days, sound nights,—oh, can there be / A life more rational and free?"
Look up the Indian pipe plant
questions: What does the first stanza say makes up 'the sum of living'?
Where was the poet's cradle?
Who does the last stanza call happy?
answers: Not what we want, but what we must do
Beside the sea
The man content to till his own field
lessons.notes: Poem by Richard Henry Stoddard.

lessons.title: Lesson CVII: The Virginians
steps: New words: patrimonial (inherited), disaffected (discontented), obsequious (too eager to please), urbanity (polished manners), epitaph (words on a tombstone)
Read the passage aloud
Talk together about how the narrator describes slavery, and what is false about it
Narrate: how were the twins George and Harry alike and different?
questions: Who were George and Harry Esmond?
How were the twins different in temper?
What did George do for his young servant that angered his mother?
answers: Twin grandsons of Mr. Esmond of Castlewood, Virginia
George was quiet, studious, and gentle; Harry loved sport and fighting
He fanned the flies off the sleeping boy instead of punishing him
lessons.notes: From 'The Virginians' by W. M. Thackeray. IMPORTANT: this passage pictures slavery as mild and enslaved people as 'lazy and not unhappy,' and uses racist terms. That is false and offensive. Preview it; you may skip it, or read it with an older child as an example of how slavery was excused and why that view was wrong.

lessons.title: Lesson CVIII: Minot's Ledge
steps: Read the poem aloud with rising tension, then quiet at the end
Find Minot's Ledge near Boston on a map
Narrate: how did the lighthouse keeper save his son?
questions: What are the clouds compared to?
Who was the keeper praying for most?
How did he pull his son from the sea?
answers: Ghostly hounds
His son Charlie, at sea
He threw a rope with grappling hooks and pulled him onto the rocks
lessons.notes: Poem by Fitz-James O'Brien, who died in the Civil War. The Minot's Ledge lighthouse was famous for being destroyed by a storm in 1851 and rebuilt.

lessons.title: Lesson CIX: Hamlet
steps: New words: truant (one who skips duty), attent (attentive), cap-a-pie (head to foot), truncheon (a short staff), beaver (the face guard of a helmet)
Read the scene aloud as a play with three or four readers; use the book's notes for old phrases
Narrate: what did Horatio and the guards see, and what will Hamlet do?
questions: Why does Hamlet joke that Horatio came for his mother's wedding?
What did the guards see on their watch?
What does Hamlet decide to do?
answers: Because his mother married again very soon after his father's funeral
A ghost that looked like Hamlet's dead father, in armor
Keep watch that night and speak to the ghost
lessons.notes: From Shakespeare's 'Hamlet,' Act I, Scene 2. A good first taste of Shakespeare; the play itself is dark and better for older students.

lessons.title: Lesson CX: Dissertation on Roast Pig
steps: New words: younkers (youngsters), antediluvian (very ancient), premonitory (giving warning), obnoxious (offensive), culinary (to do with cooking)
Read the essay aloud, enjoying Lamb's mock-serious tone
Written narration: in a paragraph, retell how roast pig was 'discovered' and why the jury said 'Not Guilty'
questions: How did Bo-bo discover roast pig?
Why did the jury find Ho-ti and Bo-bo not guilty?
What 'discovery' finally ended the house fires?
answers: He burned down the cottage with the piglets inside, burned his fingers on one, and licked them
They tasted the pig themselves
That meat could be cooked without burning down a whole house
lessons.notes: By Charles Lamb, from 'Essays of Elia.' A tall tale, not real Chinese history. A good example of humor and exaggeration.

lessons.title: Lesson CXI: A Pen Picture
steps: New words: glamour (a magic charm on the eyes), loch (a lake or arm of the sea), peat (turf burned for fuel), curlew (a shore bird), plover (a shore bird)
Read the description aloud slowly, noticing every color word
Find the Isle of Lewis in the Outer Hebrides on a map
Written narration: in a paragraph, write your own 'pen picture' of a sunset you have seen
questions: What did Lavender imagine Sheila and her father to be?
Why did Sheila say she could walk to Borvabost alone?
Name three colors Black uses for the evening sky.
answers: A princess and the King of Thule
It wouldn't get darker than the twilight all night in the north
Gold, violet, crimson, rose, pale yellow
lessons.notes: From 'A Princess of Thule' by William Black, set in the Scottish Hebrides, where summer nights are short and light.

lessons.title: Lesson CXII: The Great Voices
steps: Read the poem aloud, letting the sea, torrents, and forests 'call' to each other
Memorize: the last stanza
Talk about what nature 'says' to the human heart in the poem
questions: What does the voice from the sea say?
What do the torrents add?
How should the human heart sing, according to the last stanza?
answers: "O spirit! be glad and be free"
"O spirit! be free and be strong"
With joy like the fountains, calm as the mountains, and deep as the woods and the sea
lessons.notes: Poem by Charles T. Brooks.

lessons.title: Lesson CXIII: A Picture of Human Life
steps: New words: caravansary (an inn for travelers in the East), meanders (windings), deviations (wanderings off course), palliation (excusing), labyrinth (a maze)
Read the allegory aloud
Written narration: in a paragraph, explain how each part of Obidah's journey stands for a part of life
questions: Why did Obidah leave the main road?
What happened when he lost his way?
What hope does the hermit give at the end?
answers: The shady path through the grove seemed pleasant and looked as if it went the same way
A storm came, night fell, and wild beasts howled around him
It is never too late to turn back; a wanderer who asks God for help can still return
lessons.notes: By Samuel Johnson, from 'The Rambler.' An allegory: a story where each part stands for something else.

lessons.title: Lesson CXIV: A Summer Longing
steps: Read the poem aloud with longing, stressing the refrain 'green fields wait for me'
Memorize: the first stanza
List the summer sights and sounds the poet dreams of
questions: What refrain ends each stanza?
Name two summer sounds the poet longs to hear.
answers: (The) green fields wait for me (or thee)
Birds twittering, lowing herds, the distant sea, breezes in the reeds, insects chirping
lessons.notes: Poem by George Arnold.

lessons.title: Lesson CXV: Fate
steps: Read the short poem aloud, letting the surprise land in the last stanza
Memorize: the whole poem (12 lines)
Narrate: what is the twist?
questions: Why did the first speaker refuse to go to sea?
What happened to the ship and the hunters?
What happened to the 'safe' town?
answers: It looked stormy and dangerous
They came home safely
An earthquake swallowed it
lessons.notes: Poem by Bret Harte. A good starting point for talking about trust, risk, and providence.

lessons.title: Lesson CXVI: The Bible the Best of Classics
steps: New words: classic (a work of lasting excellence), authenticity (genuineness), sanction (authority), vindicated (defended), seraph (a high angel)
Read the speech aloud, noticing how many sentences begin 'If we...'
Written narration: in a paragraph, list the reasons Grimké gives for calling the Bible the best classic
questions: Who does the author say recorded the Bible's truths?
What blessings does he say the Bible brings on earth?
answers: The patriarch and the prophet, the evangelist and the martyr
Humility, resignation, purity, order, peace, faith, hope, and charity
lessons.notes: By Thomas S. Grimké of South Carolina. Notice the repeated 'If we...' pattern, a speaker's device called anaphora.

lessons.title: Lesson CXVII: My Mother's Bible
steps: Read the poem aloud tenderly
Look at your own family Bible or family records, if you have them
Memorize: the last stanza
Narrate: what memories does the Bible bring back to the speaker?
questions: Who gave the speaker the Bible?
What memories does it bring back?
What does the last line say the Bible taught him?
answers: His mother, as she was dying
The family gathered at the hearth after evening prayer, his father reading aloud
How to die (as well as how to live)
lessons.notes: Poem by George Pope Morris. The final lesson of the Fifth Reader.
